meta.title: Roster — An office for your coding agents
meta.description: A macOS app that turns your Claude Code sessions into little colleagues in a pixel office. They work at their desks — and walk to yours when they're done. Free, open source, local-only.

hero.title: Your coding agents just got <mark>an office</mark>.
hero.subtitle: Roster turns every Claude Code session into a little colleague in a pixel office on your Mac. They work at their desks, stand up when they need you, and walk over to yours when the job is done. You can even wander the room with your arrow keys.
hero.note: macOS 14+ · Signed & notarized · No account, no telemetry
hero.caption: Live from the room — the agents take turns walking over when they finish.
hero.hint: Psst: W·A·S·D moves your avatar (same keys, whatever the layout — Z·Q·S·D on AZERTY). T toggles the theme.

positioning.title: Not another dashboard.
positioning.body: Lists, diffs, kanban boards — other tools already do that well. Roster is the ambient version: a quiet little office in the corner of your screen. You don't read it, you glance at it. The state of the room is the state of your agents.

features.title: A room that speaks for itself

f1.title: The walk
f1.body: Real work earns a crossing: when an agent finishes a long task, it stands up, walks across the office and waits at your desk until you've had a look — with a native notification (and a ding) in case you're elsewhere. Discovering a finished agent twenty minutes late is over.

f2.title: One glance, every state
f2.body: Seated and working. Standing when it needs your input. Walking when it's done. At your desk for review. A red pill when a turn fails. Desks appear with the first session on a project — and leave with the last one.

f3.title: Click a colleague
f3.body: Click an agent — in the room or in the sidebar — and its profile card slides in: the last thing it said, the repo path, one button for VS Code, one for the Terminal, one to mark the work reviewed.

f4.title: A real little office
f4.body: The colleagues are real 3D — voxel bodies under a real light, turning toward wherever they walk. Stroll around with the arrow keys, zoom in when the room gets crowded, and toggle the sidebar for the roll call.

how.title: Three small pieces, all local

s1.title: A hook
s1.body: With your consent, Roster adds a small hook to every Claude Code settings.json it finds — each one backed up first. From then on, every session event is appended to a local spool file.

s2.title: A spool file
s2.body: Events pile up even while Roster is closed. On launch the room replays them and catches up — no server, no socket, no polling.

s3.title: A room
s3.body: Events map one-to-one to the choreography: needs-input stands the agent up, a finished long turn triggers the walk, a failure pulls it back to its station, and a closed session takes its desk along.

how.privacy: Everything stays on your Mac. Roster never reads your code — only session events. No network, no account, no telemetry.

open.title: MIT, from day one
open.body: Roster is free and open source. The state machine is unit-tested, the fragile parts are isolated behind a thin layer, and every design decision is written down in the repo — including the researched roadmap for Gemini CLI, Codex and opencode support. Good first issues are waiting for you.

q1.q: Does it work with agents other than Claude Code?
q1.a: Claude Code today. But the seam is already in the code, and the research is public in docs/providers.md: Gemini CLI is first in line (its hooks are nearly identical), then opencode and Codex.

q2.a: No. It only sees session events: state changes, the working directory, and the last assistant message for the summary. Nothing ever leaves your machine.

q3.q: Why isn't it on the Mac App Store?
q3.a: Roster needs to read ~/.claude and install its hook, which the App Store sandbox forbids. It ships as a signed, notarized DMG on GitHub Releases instead.

q4.q: What if Claude Code changes its file formats?
q4.a: The hooks Roster relies on are a documented interface, so the core is safe. The undocumented parts — the transcript bootstrap — are isolated and fail silently; worst case, the room misses a warm start.

cta.title: Give your agents a desk.
cta.body: One DMG, one hook — and your sessions become colleagues. The kind that walk over when they're done.

footer.tagline: A little office for your coding agents. They walk to your desk when they're done.
